overview: Economics/Business is a genuinely mixed case, not a lopsided one -- the opposite shape from Medicine (structurally different in 13 of 15 countries researched in this package). Across the same 15 countries, this family splits roughly evenly: structurally different in 5 (United States, United Kingdom, Netherlands, Canada, France), the same underlying mechanism with a higher bar in 4 (Italy, Germany, Spain, Turkey), and running through each country's ordinary general-admission mechanism with no dedicated overlay at all in the remaining 6 (Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, Switzerland, Singapore, Hong Kong) -- several of which required checking specifically because the destination institution (St. Gallen, SMU) is itself an economics/business-focused institution, which invites conflating 'this institution's general admission' with 'a field-specific gate.' The second, compounding finding is about the SHAPE of structural difference where it exists. Medicine's structural differences are almost always about capacity-constrained professional licensure -- a government-funded training-place ceiling, a national quota, a mandatory aptitude test tied to clinical competence. Economics/Business's structural differences, where found, are instead almost always about PRESTIGE-TIER STRATIFICATION layered on top of an otherwise open or moderately competitive field: a separate, harder-to-reach elite inner track sitting alongside ordinary access to the same broad subject. The clearest examples: France's prepa ECG/ECT to BCE/Ecricome concours pathway runs alongside an open, non-selective Licence Economie-Gestion in the very same country; several elite US universities gate their named business school as its own freshman-application object while Business/Economics as a general field of study remains ordinary at most other US universities; the UK's TMUA applies at a defined cluster of quantitatively-elite departments (Cambridge, LSE, Imperial, UCL) while most UK Economics programmes require no test at all; the Netherlands numerus-fixus-caps the English/international track of Economics and Business Economics at UvA while the identical Dutch-taught track of the SAME programme stays open-admission; Canada's leading Commerce programmes (Queen's Smith, Rotman, Sauder, Schulich) layer a mandatory, rubric-scored, real-time video-and-written supplementary application on top of ordinary grades-based review, a genuinely different evidence-collection mechanism from an activities list. Nowhere in this family does a government cap the total number of Economics/Business training places the way the UK and Australia cap Medicine places, and nowhere does Economics/Business require a dedicated national aptitude test analogous to UCAT or HPAT -- the structural differences that do exist are elite-tier access mechanisms, not field-wide capacity or licensure gates.

countries.scope: institution-specific -- a patchwork of named business schools with their own admissions object, not a national or even majority pattern
countries.description: At a defined, non-universal cluster of US universities, undergraduate Business is not a major a student declares after enrolling -- it is a separate school with its own admissions gate, evaluated apart from (sometimes instead of, sometimes in addition to) the general university admission most other US applicants experience. This is a genuinely different admissions OBJECT, not a stricter version of the general Common App / holistic-review model already documented for the US, but the specific mechanism varies sharply even among the three named universities checked this pass. (1) University of Texas at Austin's McCombs School runs direct-admit-to-major at the freshman application itself: applicants list a specific BBA major, McCombs evaluates them apart from (more selectively than) UT's automatic-admission baseline, at roughly a 9-10% acceptance rate against UT's much higher overall admit rate; students not directly admitted can pursue internal transfer later via a defined 30-credit-hour Business Foundations coursework track (Calculus I/II, Micro/Macro, BA 101/102). (2) Indiana University's Kelley School announced a genuine, dated mechanism CHANGE effective fall 2026: previously a narrower/more metric-driven direct-admit pool, now EVERY applicant who indicates a Kelley major is considered for direct admission through a comprehensive holistic academic review (course rigor, especially quantitative subjects) at the point of the freshman application itself -- letters of recommendation were explicitly dropped from the evaluation. Students not directly admitted may still join Kelley after one year with defined course/GPA requirements. (3) Michigan's Ross School underwent the sharpest recent shift: through fall 2024, Ross was reachable ONLY via 'Preferred Admission' -- a two-step process requiring admission to another Michigan school (Engineering, Kinesiology, Music/Theatre/Dance, or Stamps Art & Design) first, with transfer into Ross in year two. Starting fall 2025, Ross became a First-Year Admitting Unit on the Common App, meaning direct freshman admission to Ross now exists alongside continued (narrower) Preferred Admission from a smaller set of other schools -- but this traded away a former safety net: students who apply directly to Ross and are rejected no longer have the fallback of being admitted to LSA instead, since Preferred Admission via the College of Engineering route to Ross was eliminated. All three differ from most US universities, where Business/Economics is an ordinary major requiring nothing beyond the general application already documented for the US country doc -- this is a genuinely institution-specific phenomenon, not a national one, and the specific mechanism (direct-admit-to-major vs. holistic-review vs. recently-added-direct-with-a-narrowing-transfer-safety-net) differs meaningfully across the three schools checked, so none of the three should be treated as representative of how 'US direct-admit business school' works generally.
countries.eligibility_determinants: At direct-admit schools: GPA, course rigor (especially Calculus AB/BC and other quantitative coursework), class rank, and standardized test scores where required by the parent university, evaluated at the point of the freshman application specifically for the named business school rather than for the university generally. Kelley's fall-2026 shift explicitly reweights toward coursework rigor and away from recommendation letters. For students who miss direct admission: a defined internal-transfer coursework/GPA threshold completed during year one (McCombs' Business Foundations model; Kelley's one-year-then-reapply model).
countries.strengthens_application: Demonstrated quantitative rigor (Calculus, statistics, economics coursework) and, where the school evaluates it, articulated fit with a specific BBA major rather than 'business' as a generic interest -- McCombs explicitly rewards applicants who can explain why a specific major (Finance, Marketing, MIS, etc.), not just the school generally. Where a direct-admit school still exists as a distinct gate, being admitted directly avoids the more uncertain, capacity-limited internal-transfer route later.
countries.largely_irrelevant: General extracurricular breadth unconnected to demonstrated quantitative/business-adjacent depth; for Kelley specifically as of the fall 2026 change, recommendation letters are no longer part of the evaluation at all -- a genuine, dated policy fact that should not be assumed to hold at other business schools or at Kelley in earlier cycles.
countries.never_infer: Never assume one named business school's mechanism (direct-admit-to-major, holistic freshman review, or preferred-admission-then-transfer) generalizes to another -- McCombs, Kelley, and Ross are three genuinely different shapes, confirmed independently this pass, not three examples of one pattern. Never assume Ross's current (fall-2025-onward) direct-admission option means the former transfer-only safety net (LSA fallback) still exists -- it was explicitly removed as part of the same change. Never treat Kelley's fall-2026 process as the process in effect for any cycle before it; this is an active, dated, recently-announced change, not a long-standing steady state, and should be reconfirmed each cycle. Never assume a university that lacks a named, separately-gated business school (the majority of US universities) has any Business-specific admissions mechanism at all -- for most US institutions, Business/Economics is an ordinary major following the general US admissions model already documented in this package.

countries.scope: programme/institution-specific -- a defined cluster of quantitatively-elite departments, not a national Economics requirement
countries.description: General UK admission (already documented) runs on predicted-then-confirmed grades against a UCAS conditional offer, one shared personal statement, and no test for most subjects. At a defined cluster of universities, Economics specifically adds a mandatory pre-interview quantitative admissions test the general model has none of -- but which specific test, and whether it is mandatory or merely reward-bearing, genuinely differs by institution, and the same-sounding requirement splits into two DIFFERENT tests depending on which flagship university a student targets. TMUA (Test of Mathematics for University Admission) is the central pre-interview test for Cambridge Economics and is mandatory for LSE Economics (2027 entry); Imperial requires it for Economics, Finance and Data Science; UCL requires it specifically for its Economics BSc (Econ) and Economics with a Year Abroad BSc (Econ) degrees. Warwick and Durham instead treat a strong TMUA score as reward-bearing (a reduced offer) rather than mandatory. Oxford's Economics-adjacent courses -- PPE, Economics and Management, History and Economics -- do NOT use TMUA at all: for 2027 entry Oxford introduced an entirely new test, TARA (Test of Academic Reasoning for Admissions, replacing the discontinued TSA), specifically for these courses plus Human Sciences and the Psychology-adjacent courses -- a three-module (Critical Thinking, Problem Solving, Writing Task) computer-based test delivered via Pearson VUE. A counselor defaulting a Cambridge-Economics-track student's TMUA preparation onto an Oxford PPE applicant, or vice versa, would prepare the wrong test entirely -- these are not two names for the same instrument.
countries.eligibility_determinants: The general UK predicted-grade/A-Level-or-IB baseline plus, at the specific universities and courses named above, a qualifying TMUA or TARA score sat on its own fixed calendar ahead of the general UCAS deadline. LSE BSc Economics additionally requires A* specifically in Mathematics (A*AA overall, or IB 39pts/766 HL incl. 7 in Maths) per the existing UK country doc -- Mathematics is a hard subject prerequisite at the most selective Economics departments, not merely 'assumed knowledge.'
countries.strengthens_application: A strong TMUA score at the universities that weight or require it (roughly 6.0+ competitive at Imperial/LSE/UCL per current guidance) or a strong TARA score for Oxford's Economics-adjacent courses; beyond the test layer, the general UK 'super-curricular' framing already documented (subject-adjacent depth over general breadth) applies unchanged.
countries.largely_irrelevant: General extracurricular breadth, exactly as for UK admission generally; at the majority of UK universities offering Economics -- outside the Cambridge/LSE/Imperial/UCL/Warwick/Durham/Oxford cluster -- no test of any kind is required, and treating TMUA/TARA as a universal UK Economics requirement would be a real error.
countries.never_infer: Never treat TMUA and TARA as interchangeable or as two names for the same test -- they are administered by different bodies, cover different content, and apply to different universities' Economics-adjacent courses (TMUA: Cambridge, LSE, Imperial, UCL Economics specifically, Warwick/Durham as reward-bearing; TARA: Oxford's PPE/Economics and Management/History and Economics only). Never assume a mandatory-vs-reward-bearing status generalizes across universities -- the same test is mandatory at some and merely score-boosting at others. Never assume this cluster of test-requiring universities represents how UK Economics admission works nationally; most UK Economics programmes require no admissions test.

countries.scope: programme/track-specific -- can vary within the SAME programme at the SAME university, by language track alone
countries.description: General Dutch Bachelor's admission (already documented) is eligibility-threshold-based: VWO-equivalence plus subject prerequisites equals admission for open programmes, with numerus fixus as the exception mechanism. Economics/Business is a genuine, confirmed exception field at several universities -- but the sharpest finding this pass is that the SAME named programme, at the SAME university, teaching the SAME content, can be open in one language track and numerus fixus in the other. UvA's Economics and Business Economics Bachelor's runs two tracks: the Dutch track has NO selection procedure at all (numerus fixus does not apply), while the English track is capped at 850 first-year places and requires passing a selection test assessing Mathematics, Economics, and Principles of Economics and Business -- confirmed directly on UvA's own programme pages. This is a materially different shape from Italy's Medicine language-bifurcation (documented in this package's Medicine research), where BOTH instruction-language tracks were still restricted, just via different mechanisms -- here, one track is genuinely open-admission and the other genuinely capped, for identical content. Beyond UvA, Erasmus School of Economics' International Bachelor Economics and Business Economics (IBEB) is a confirmed numerus fixus programme (700 places for 2026-27), using a hybrid mechanism: the best-ranked applicants (via grades plus a curriculum-based activity/test) receive the first 350 ranking numbers directly, the remainder are allocated via weighted lottery. Tilburg's BSc Economics is also numerus fixus, ranked by average grade, a knowledge test, and possibly a motivation letter. UvA's PPLE (Politics, Psychology, Law and Economics) is numerus fixus at roughly 300 places against several thousand applicants, using grades, a motivation letter, and an online assessment. Economics/Business is therefore one of the more commonly-capped non-health fields in the Dutch system -- a genuine correction to any assumption that only Medicine-adjacent fields carry numerus fixus.
countries.eligibility_determinants: The general VWO-equivalence/subject-prerequisite baseline (Economie & Maatschappij profiel or the foreign-curriculum equivalent) to be eligible at all; beyond that, at each numerus-fixus programme, that programme's own ranking inputs -- UvA English-track's selection test, Erasmus IBEB's curriculum-based-activity-plus-lottery hybrid, Tilburg's grade-plus-knowledge-test-plus-motivation-letter formula, or PPLE's grades-plus-motivation-letter-plus-assessment combination. Which specific mechanism applies is programme- and even track-specific, not predictable from 'Economics in the Netherlands' as a category.
countries.strengthens_application: At numerus-fixus Economics/Business programmes, strong performance on the programme's own selection instrument (UvA's Maths/Economics test, Tilburg's knowledge test) and, where a motivation letter is one of the legally-required qualitative criteria (Tilburg, PPLE), a demonstrated, specific fit rationale. At UvA's Dutch-track Economics and Business Economics and at any other open programme, nothing beyond meeting the eligibility threshold -- eligible functionally equals admitted, exactly as RULE-ADMISSIONS-001 already establishes for open Dutch programmes generally.
countries.largely_irrelevant: General extracurricular breadth at open-admission tracks (irrelevant, since eligible equals admitted); at numerus-fixus tracks, activity unconnected to the specific tested competencies (quantitative reasoning, economics aptitude) or, where required, the motivation letter's own stated criteria.
countries.never_infer: Never assume 'Economics and Business Economics at UvA' is uniformly open or uniformly capped -- it is both, simultaneously, split purely by which language track a student enters, for identical content. Never assume a Dutch Economics/Business programme is open by default the way most non-Medicine Dutch Bachelor's programmes are -- Erasmus IBEB, Tilburg Economics, and UvA's English-track Economics and Business Economics, and PPLE are all confirmed capped. Never assume the specific selection method (test-only, hybrid lottery, motivation-letter-weighted) generalizes from one numerus-fixus Economics/Business programme to another -- each was independently confirmed to use a different combination this pass.

countries.scope: institution-specific -- confirmed common among several leading Commerce/Business programmes, not a national feature and not universal even among elite programmes
countries.description: General Canadian undergraduate admission (already documented) is predominantly grades/transcript-based, with essay requirements genuinely varying by university -- U of T's general Arts & Science reviews transcript only, while UBC's Personal Profile is a well-documented, heavily-weighted exception. Several of Canada's leading Commerce/Business programmes sharpen this exception into its own distinct pattern: a MANDATORY supplementary application built on a TIMED, rubric-scored WRITTEN-PLUS-VIDEO response format (commonly delivered via the Kira Talent platform), evaluating durable traits demonstrated in the moment rather than a retrospective activities inventory. Queen's Smith School of Business (Commerce) confirms this directly: applicants complete a timed written response and a timed video response (2 minutes to prepare, 2 minutes to record, one randomly-drawn question from a small prompt bank), scored against an official rubric assessing description of challenge, initiative, problem-solving ability, and reflection -- explicitly NOT a review of an activities list. This is not a Queen's-specific outlier: the identical structural shape (mandatory, timed, video-plus-written, rubric-scored, assessing leadership/resilience/teamwork/problem-solving) recurs at the University of Toronto's Rotman Commerce (a mandatory supplemental application meaningfully weighted alongside grades), UBC Sauder's BCom (a 'Personal Profile' combining short written responses and a video interview), and York's Schulich BBA (video interview responses, a timed written essay, and a leadership profile, explicitly weighted EQUALLY with high-school academics). Western's Ivey Business School uses a third, different shape again: a delayed 'Advanced Entry Opportunity' -- entered from high school but not formally admitted to Ivey until year three, via its own competitive process (already documented in the existing Canada country doc). By contrast, no equivalent supplementary-application requirement was found for McGill's Desautels BCom in sources reviewed this pass -- a genuine, lower-confidence gap rather than a confirmed absence, but a real signal that even among Canada's most prominent Commerce programmes this model, while common, is not universal.
countries.eligibility_determinants: The general Canadian admission-average/prerequisite baseline (competitive averages commonly in the high-80s to mid-90s at the programmes researched) to be considered at all, PLUS, at the programmes using this model, a passing/competitive score on the timed written-and-video supplementary application, assessed independently from and, at Schulich specifically, weighted equally with the academic average.
countries.strengthens_application: Demonstrated initiative, adaptability/resilience, structured problem-solving, and reflective self-awareness, shown through real-time constructed responses to a novel prompt -- not through a longer or more decorated activities list. Because the prompts are drawn from a small bank and answered live, rehearsed or generic answers are explicitly a weaker signal than clear, specific, reflective ones; content and clarity are what is scored, not delivery style, tone, or presentation (Queen's states explicitly that appearance/tone are not part of the evaluation).
countries.largely_irrelevant: The length or breadth of a student's activities list on its own -- these programmes are not reviewing an inventory the way a US Common App or NUS's structured achievements list does; a thin activities list attached to a strong, specific, reflective video/written response can outperform a long list attached to a generic one. At McGill's Desautels (where no equivalent mechanism was found), the general Canadian pattern of transcript-driven review appears to apply instead, though this was not exhaustively confirmed.
countries.never_infer: Never assume Queen's Commerce's video-and-written supplementary model is a one-school outlier -- the identical structural shape (timed, rubric-scored, real-time-constructed-response, assessing initiative/resilience/problem-solving) is confirmed at Rotman Commerce, UBC Sauder, and Schulich BBA as well, making it the more common pattern among Canada's leading Commerce programmes, not an exception. Never assume this model is universal across ALL Canadian Business programmes -- McGill Desautels shows no confirmed equivalent, and Western Ivey uses a different, delayed-admission shape entirely. Never treat this as a general Canadian admissions feature -- it is specific to Commerce/Business programmes at the universities that use it; the same universities' other general-admission faculties (e.g., U of T's general Arts & Science) do not use an equivalent mechanism.

countries.scope: national consortium (BCE, Ecricome) + programme (individual CPGE ECG/ECT prepa and target Grande Ecole) -- structurally distinct from, and running alongside, ordinary Licence Economie-Gestion
countries.description: This resolves the lead directly: France's Grandes Ecoles de Commerce are reached through an elite parallel pathway with the identical dual-stage SHAPE as engineering's CPGE-to-concours system, but running through entirely separate, business-school-specific institutions and consortia -- not a subset or variant of the engineering pathway. Entry into the 2-year 'classe preparatoire economique et commerciale' (CPGE ECG, the general track, or ECT, the technological-Bac track) happens exactly like engineering CPGE: via Parcoursup, on academic dossier only (premiere/terminale grades, teacher appreciations, a short motivation statement), evaluated by a commission of the prepa's own teachers with no ranking algorithm -- confirmed as one of Parcoursup's 'formations selectives,' the same procedural category as engineering CPGE, categorically different from ordinary non-selective Licences. The genuine restriction does not bite at this entry point: it bites two years later, at a separate, high-stakes 'concours' run entirely outside Parcoursup by inter-school exam consortia -- and there are confirmed to be (at least) two parallel, non-overlapping business-school consortia, mirroring engineering's own plurality of concours (Mines-Ponts, Centrale-Supelec, e3a, etc.). The BCE (Banque Commune d'Epreuves), run by the Paris Ile-de-France Chamber of Commerce and Industry, gives access to 18 schools including the 'trio de tete' HEC Paris, ESSEC, and ESCP, plus EDHEC, emlyon, Audencia, SKEMA and others -- written exams run roughly mid-April to end of May, followed by oral exams roughly mid-June to early July (2026 cycle), with admissibility, oral, and final-admission results released on staggered dates per school. Ecricome is a SEPARATE, non-overlapping 5-school consortium (EM Strasbourg, KEDGE, Montpellier Business School, NEOMA, Rennes School of Business), on its own staggered calendar so a candidate can sit both; Ecricome added new parallel-entry voies for 2026 (a D1/D2 track for literary-prepa students and a scientific-prepa track) alongside its core ECG/ECT voie. This entire structure runs alongside, not instead of, an ordinary, open, Parcoursup-direct Licence Economie-Gestion -- already documented in the existing France country doc as one of the named 'licences en tension' fields (nominally non-selective, softly ranked by attendus-fit only when locally oversubscribed under the 2018 loi ORE) -- meaning a French student's path into 'Economics/Business' bifurcates as sharply by CHOSEN PATHWAY as an engineering-track student's does, into either an open/soft-ranked university Licence or a genuinely selective, two-stage prepa-then-concours elite track, both nominally in the same broad subject area.
countries.eligibility_determinants: For CPGE ECG/ECT entry: the same premiere/terminale dossier evidence as engineering CPGE, evaluated by the prepa's own admissions commission, not an algorithm. For the actual concours (BCE or Ecricome) two years later: written examination performance across the prepa's own subject coefficients (mathematics, economics/social science, languages, a general-knowledge essay, etc.), which determines 'admissibilite' (eligibility to sit the oral round), followed by oral examination performance, which determines final admission and school ranking. For ordinary Licence Economie-Gestion: the same non-selective/attendus-fit mechanism as any other 'licence en tension,' evaluated via Parcoursup, with no concours involved at all.
countries.strengthens_application: For CPGE entry: a strong dossier in mathematics plus demonstrated interest in social science/current economic affairs -- the prepa's own published 'attendus.' For the concours itself: sustained two-year performance across the prepa's demanding coefficient structure, oral performance at admissibility, and (per general CPGE pattern already noted in the France country doc) the choice to sit BOTH BCE and Ecricome on their staggered calendars to maximize the number of schools a candidate can be ranked against.
countries.largely_irrelevant: For ordinary Licence Economie-Gestion: essentially the same factors already documented as largely absent from French Licence admission generally (recommendation letters, broad extracurricular activity) -- this is not a Business-specific finding, it inherits directly from the general French pattern. For CPGE/concours entry: general extracurricular breadth unconnected to the tested academic subjects carries little confirmed weight in the concours's own written/oral scoring.
countries.never_infer: Never treat 'Grande Ecole de Commerce' admission as a subset or lighter variant of engineering's CPGE-concours system -- they are structurally parallel (same two-stage shape) but run through entirely separate prepa tracks (ECG/ECT vs. MPSI/PCSI/MP/PC/PSI etc.) and entirely separate, non-overlapping concours consortia (BCE and Ecricome vs. Mines-Ponts, Centrale-Supelec, e3a, X-ENS, etc.) leading to different named schools. Never assume passing into CPGE ECG/ECT is equivalent to admission to a Grande Ecole -- exactly as the existing France country doc already warns for engineering, the entry-level dossier-based CPGE selection and the much more consequential concours two years later are two different events with two different mechanisms, and conflating them materially overstates how far along a CPGE-track student already is. Never assume ordinary Licence Economie-Gestion carries the same selectivity as the CPGE/concours pathway -- it is the open, Parcoursup-direct, softly-ranked-only-when-oversubscribed route documented generally for 'licences en tension,' a fundamentally lower-stakes single-stage process.

countries.scope: university -- individual institutions choose to cap Economics locally, using the same national test family as everywhere else
countries.description: Economics runs through the identical CISIA TOLC test-family mechanism already documented for the general Italian model, with a dedicated TOLC-Economics variant among the family's subject-specific tests (alongside Engineering, Pharmacy, Humanities, Sciences, Biology, Psychology, Political/Social Sciences, Agriculture/Veterinary). Exactly as for the general model: at OPEN Economics programmes, the test is a non-binding orientation/placement check (a low score can trigger the OFA remedial module, not a denial); at programmes an individual university chooses to cap under 'numero programmato locale,' the identical test becomes the binding, ranked selection criterion. This is a university-level decision, not a national one -- Economics is explicitly named (alongside Engineering, Architecture, Psychology, Communication) as one of the fields individual universities commonly choose to cap locally, varying institution-by-institution and year-by-year, with no nationally uniform list. No dedicated, Economics-specific test, quota, or interview layer beyond this existing TOLC mechanism was found.
countries.eligibility_determinants: The secondary diploma (12-year threshold, as for any Italian programme) plus, at any university that has locally capped Economics that cycle, a competitive rank on the TOLC-Economics/CEnT-S score -- the same instrument used as a non-binding check at open Economics programmes.
countries.strengthens_application: A strong TOLC-Economics/CEnT-S score, at whichever universities have locally capped the programme that cycle -- the same lever the general Italian model already documents for any locally-capped field.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Personal statements, recommendation letters, and general extracurricular breadth -- absent from Italian Economics admission for the same reasons already documented for Italian admission generally (a qualification/test-threshold model with no structural place for narrative evidence).
countries.never_infer: Never assume Economics is capped nationally in Italy the way Medicine is -- it is a purely local, university-by-university, year-by-year decision, and 'numero programmato locale' status at one university does not imply the same at another. Never assume the TOLC-Economics score functions differently from any other locally-capped-field TOLC variant -- it is the identical instrument playing the identical dual orientation/binding-ranking role documented for the general Italian model.

countries.scope: university -- local NC (ortlicher Numerus Clausus), the decentralized layer, not hochschulstart's national NC
countries.description: Business Administration (Betriebswirtschaftslehre/BWL) is one of the most commonly-cited examples of a subject placed under LOCAL NC by individual German universities -- but local NC is explicitly documented as a different layer from, and the same threshold-based Abiturnote mechanism as, the rest of German direct-entry admission, just with a university-set, self-defined, fluctuating cutoff that responds purely to that specific institution's demand that cycle. This is categorically different from Medicine's national NC: hochschulstart's centrally-coordinated quota system (Abiturbestenquote/AdH/ZEQ) is confirmed to cover exactly four subjects -- Human Medicine, Dentistry, Veterinary Medicine, Pharmacy -- and Business/Economics is not, and has never been, one of them. No dedicated German aptitude test analogous to TMS/HAM-Nat, and no national quota structure, was found for Business/Economics anywhere in sources reviewed.
countries.eligibility_determinants: The general Abiturnote/HZB-equivalence threshold, plus, at any specific university that has set a local NC for its BWL or Economics programme that cycle, a competitive rank against that university's own self-defined threshold -- which can differ sharply between two universities offering the identically-named subject, exactly as documented for local NC generally.
countries.strengthens_application: Nothing beyond the Abiturnote itself and whatever narrow additional criteria (a subject-specific grade component, occasionally an interview or aptitude element) the specific university publishes for its own local-NC procedure -- there is no confirmed nationally-uniform lever.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Personal statements, recommendation letters, and general extracurricular activity -- absent from German Business/Economics admission for the same reasons already documented generally for German direct-entry admission.
countries.never_infer: Never conflate local NC (Business/Economics' actual mechanism) with the national NC quota system that governs Medicine, Dentistry, Veterinary Medicine, and Pharmacy specifically -- they are different layers with different governance, and Business/Economics has never been part of the national layer. Never assume a local-NC threshold at one university generalizes to another university's identically-named programme.

countries.scope: national formula (nota de acceso/nota de admision) executed regionally -- the identical mechanism as every other public Grado, with an unconfirmed private-sector caveat
countries.description: Administracion y Direccion de Empresas (ADE) and Economia run through the literally identical nota de acceso/nota de admision formula and regional Distrito Unico ranked-allocation mechanism as every other public Grado -- no separate national test, quota system, or interview layer was found, the same clean pattern already confirmed for Spain's public-track Medicine in this package's Medicine research. What makes top ADE programmes restrictive is purely a high, demand-driven nota de corte: confirmed for the 2025-26 cycle at roughly 11.9-12.0 (out of 14) at Universidad Complutense de Madrid and roughly 11.0-11.5 at Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, depending on campus -- high, but not approaching Medicine's illustrative 11.4-13.4 range, consistent with ADE being competitive-but-not-extreme relative to Spain's most restricted field. As with Medicine, private universities plausibly run separate ADE/Business admissions processes with their own tests/interviews (by direct structural analogy to the confirmed private-Medicine finding in this package), but this was not independently verified for Business specifically this pass -- flagged as an assumption-by-analogy, not a confirmed finding, following the same discipline already established for Medicine's private-sector caveat.
countries.eligibility_determinants: The nota de admision itself -- EBAU (or UNEDasiss's PCE for the international track) results, weighted per the university's own chosen ponderacion subjects (commonly Mathematics for ADE-type degrees) -- ranked against the regional Distrito Unico's that-cycle capacity for the specific programme.
countries.strengthens_application: A high nota de admision, boosted by scoring well in whichever subjects the target university has chosen to weight at 0.1-0.2 for that degree -- the same lever as any other competitive Spanish public Grado, nothing ADE-specific.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Personal statements, recommendation letters, and general extracurricular activity -- absent from Spanish public ADE/Economics admission for the same reasons already documented generally for the Spanish formula-driven system.
countries.never_infer: Never assume a private Spanish university's ADE/Business admissions process mirrors the public nota-de-corte mechanism -- private institutions plausibly run separate processes (as confirmed for Medicine), but this was not independently verified for Business this pass and should not be assumed true by analogy alone. Never treat one cycle's nota de corte as predictive of a future cycle's -- it is a self-adjusting, demand-driven figure recalculated every year, exactly as documented for the general Spanish model.

countries.scope: national -- the EA (Esit Agirlik) score-type pool, identical mechanism and formula as every other EA-track lisans programme
countries.description: Confirmed directly: Iktisat (Economics) and Isletme (Business Administration) are placed via YKS's EA (Esit Agirlik/Equal-Weight) score type -- the same score-type cluster the existing Turkey country doc already names for Law, Economics, Business, Psychology, and Social Work -- computed from the identical (TYT x 0.40) + (AYT x 0.60) + (OBP x 0.12 or 0.06) national formula and placed by the identical centralized rank-order algorithm as every other lisans programme. No dedicated test, interview, portfolio, or other non-score element exists for Economics/Business anywhere in the domestic pathway -- confirmed consistent with the existing country doc's own finding that 'Medicine, Law, top Engineering programmes remain pure score-ranked placement with no interview or portfolio step at all,' which extends identically to top Economics/Business programmes. What varies is purely the cutoff: Bogazici University's Isletme (English-taught) carried a 2025 taban puani of 495.76/500 (national success rank approximately 578th), an extreme but not maximum cutoff -- confirming the 'numerically stricter only' pattern already anticipated for this lead, with a real, sourced number rather than an assumption.
countries.eligibility_determinants: A candidate's EA-type YKS score alone, ranked nationally against every other candidate who listed the same programme code -- a candidate whose profile sits in a different score type (SAY, SOZ, DIL) cannot be placed into an EA-only-ranked Economics/Business programme regardless of any other evidence, exactly as the existing country doc documents for score-type routing generally.
countries.strengthens_application: Nothing beyond a higher EA score -- there is no named non-exam-score lever for Economics/Business, matching the 'zero channel exists for [non-academic] evidence to matter' finding already established generally for the Turkish domestic pathway.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Extracurricular activity, leadership, research, essays, and recommendations -- structurally absent from domestic-pathway placement for Economics/Business exactly as for every other lisans programme nationally; this is not a Business-specific finding, it inherits directly from the general Turkish domestic-pathway finding already established in this package.
countries.never_infer: Never assume a Turkish EA-track applicant's non-academic profile (leadership, activities, research) has any bearing on Economics/Business placement -- zero channel exists, exactly as already established for the domestic pathway generally. Never assume the specific 2025 Bogazici Isletme cutoff (495.76, rank ~578) is stable across cycles -- like every YKS cutoff, it is a self-adjusting, demand-driven figure recalculated annually. Never conflate this domestic EA-track mechanism with the separate foreign-national pathway, where Economics/Business applicants are evaluated independently by each university using TR-YOS or an accepted alternative, exactly as documented for the general Turkish foreign-national pathway.

countries.scope: national (CAO/points route for EU/EFTA/UK-fee-status applicants) -- no Business-specific overlay found, unlike Medicine's HPAT or Art & Design's portfolio
countries.description: Business/Commerce/Economics at Irish universities (Trinity Business School, UCD's business college, and others) was not found to carry any dedicated test, interview, or portfolio requirement within the domestic CAO/points route -- it runs through the same Leaving Certificate points mechanism (best 6 subjects plus any Mathematics bonus) as the large majority of Irish undergraduate courses, a sharp contrast to Medicine's nationally-uniform HPAT-plus-points formula or Art & Design's portfolio-based 'Restricted' category already documented in this package. Subject prerequisites apply the ordinary way (commonly a named Higher Level Mathematics minimum, consistent with the general pattern UCD's own non-EU table already shows varying by programme). The separate non-EU/direct-application route already documented generally for Ireland (essay-and-reference-bearing, evaluating predicted scores) would apply to a Business applicant the same way it applies to any other non-EU-route programme at that university -- not a Business-specific overlay, a route-level fact inherited from the general Irish finding.
countries.eligibility_determinants: Leaving Certificate points from the best 6 subjects (plus the national Higher Level Mathematics bonus where applicable) for EU/EFTA/UK-fee-status applicants via CAO; for non-EU/direct-route applicants, whatever predicted-grade/essay/reference package the specific university's international office requires, exactly as documented generally for the non-EU pathway.
countries.strengthens_application: A higher CAO points total and, where relevant, the national Higher Level Mathematics bonus -- no confirmed Business-specific lever beyond what the general Irish points mechanism already provides.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Essays, recommendation letters, and interviews within the domestic CAO/points route -- structurally absent for Business exactly as for the large majority of Irish CAO-route courses, inheriting directly from the general Irish finding rather than being a Business-specific result.
countries.never_infer: Never assume Business/Commerce carries a dedicated aptitude test or portfolio requirement analogous to Medicine's HPAT or Art & Design's CAO 'Restricted' flag -- none was found. Never assume the domestic CAO-route finding (no essay, no interview) extends to the separate non-EU/direct-application route, which already runs a materially different, evidence-richer evaluation for any subject, Business included.

countries.scope: state-based ATAR/selection-rank mechanism -- no confirmed dedicated Business/Commerce test, interview, or CSP-style funding exception
countries.description: Business/Commerce at Go8 and other Australian universities was not found to carry any dedicated admissions test, interview, or government funding-mechanism exception -- it runs through the same floating ATAR/selection-rank mechanism as the large majority of Australian undergraduate programmes, already documented as demand-driven and re-set every cycle rather than a fixed threshold. This is a sharp contrast to Medicine's confirmed exception: Commonwealth Supported Place funding for Business, as for most Australian fields, is allocated to universities in dollars (not fixed government-set place-counts the way Medicine's CSP allocation is), meaning Business's capacity constraint operates entirely through ordinary ATAR-cutoff competition rather than through a categorically different funding mechanism. No UCAT-ANZ/ISAT-style dedicated test or Medicine-style structured interview was found for standard-entry Business/Commerce in sources reviewed.
countries.eligibility_determinants: ATAR or selection rank (domestic) or the equivalent direct-application transcript/qualification review (most overseas-qualification holders, per the general Australian pattern already documented), plus any programme-level subject prerequisite or assumed-knowledge expectation (commonly Mathematics) a specific Business/Commerce programme publishes.
countries.strengthens_application: A higher ATAR/selection rank and meeting any stated Mathematics prerequisite or assumed-knowledge expectation -- the same levers as any other competitive-but-uncapped Australian programme, nothing Business-specific confirmed.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Personal statements and interviews for standard-entry Business/Commerce -- absent for the same reasons already documented generally for Australian admission outside Medicine/Dentistry and a small number of named bonus-points schemes.
countries.never_infer: Never assume Business/Commerce shares Medicine's CSP funding exception (a fixed government-set place-count) -- Business funding, like most Australian fields, is dollars-based with universities setting their own place mix, a categorically different mechanism from Medicine's. Never assume a high published ATAR cutoff at a prestigious Business programme implies a fixed cap or dedicated test -- it is the ordinary floating, demand-driven ATAR mechanism, the same shape as any other popular uncapped Australian course.

countries.scope: national Rank Score/University Entrance mechanism -- Business/Commerce not named among NZ's restricted-programme list
countries.description: Business/Commerce is not among the programmes New Zealand's existing country doc identifies as restricted (Medicine, Pharmacy, Nursing, Engineering, and some Law specifically) -- it was not found to carry any dedicated test, interview, or gateway-year mechanism, and instead runs through the ordinary single-stage, graduated Rank Score threshold (built from NCEA-credit accumulation, or the equivalent UE pathway for foreign-curriculum applicants) already documented as the general New Zealand undergraduate admission model. No New Zealand-specific research beyond the existing country doc's own general findings was independently conducted for Business/Commerce this pass, since no lead or contrary signal surfaced during this family's research to suggest a Business-specific mechanism exists.
countries.eligibility_determinants: University Entrance (the national floor) plus a competitive Rank Score against whichever threshold the specific university/programme publishes for Business/Commerce -- the same mechanism as most named NZ Bachelor's programmes.
countries.strengthens_application: A higher Rank Score, built from stronger NCEA Achievement-Standard credit accumulation, or the equivalent for foreign-curriculum applicants -- no Business-specific lever was found.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Personal statements and interviews -- absent for Business/Commerce for the same reasons already documented generally for New Zealand's non-restricted Bachelor's programmes.
countries.never_infer: Never assume Business/Commerce carries a gateway-year or dedicated-test mechanism analogous to Medicine's Health Sciences First Year/UCAT ANZ structure -- no such mechanism was found. This entry relies more heavily on the existing country doc's general findings than on fresh Business-specific verification this pass -- treat as inherited confidence, not independently re-confirmed.

countries.scope: institution-specific nuance -- St. Gallen's distinctive foreign-quota mechanism is confirmed to be HSG's general, nationality-triggered mechanism, not an Economics/Business-specific gate
countries.description: This resolves the lead directly, and the answer is a genuinely informative near-miss. St. Gallen's distinctive foreign-applicant selection procedure (a computer-based online aptitude test, a roughly-10-minute recorded video interview, and an English-taught Assessment Year) -- already documented in the existing Switzerland country doc as triggered by the law-mandated 25% foreign-student quota -- is confirmed directly on HSG's own admissions pages to apply IDENTICALLY across all of HSG's programmes: Economics, Business, Law, and International Affairs alike, gated by nationality/certificate-origin, not by academic field. A Law applicant to HSG faces the literally identical procedure as an Economics applicant. Because St. Gallen is itself an almost entirely business/economics/law-focused institution, most students encountering this mechanism ARE headed toward Business/Economics -- but the mechanism itself is not a field-specific gate, it is a general-HSG, nationality-triggered one, exactly the distinction the lead asked to verify. Separately, at Switzerland's other major Business/Economics faculties -- University of Zurich, HEC Lausanne, HEC Geneve -- no dedicated numerus clausus, aptitude test, or quota comparable to St. Gallen's was found in sources reviewed this pass; these appear to follow the general Swiss threshold-based Matura-equivalence model already documented for most non-Medicine Swiss Bachelor's fields, though this was not exhaustively confirmed against each institution's own primary admissions pages. At the whole-country family level, then, Economics/Business in Switzerland is best read as running through whichever general mechanism its target institution already uses -- HSG's distinctive but non-field-specific foreign-quota procedure, or the ordinary Swiss threshold-based model elsewhere -- rather than carrying its own dedicated Economics/Business mechanism.
countries.eligibility_determinants: At St. Gallen: the general HSG foreign-quota selection procedure (aptitude test, video interview, Assessment Year) for non-automatically-recognized foreign qualifications, identical across all HSG fields -- not an Economics/Business-specific determinant. At other Swiss universities' Business/Economics faculties: the general foreign-qualification recognition template already documented (mathematics, a science, and the language of instruction as examined subjects, plus four more studied subjects, commonly ~70% average).
countries.strengthens_application: At St. Gallen: performance on the general HSG aptitude test and video interview -- the same lever any HSG applicant in any field has, not an Economics/Business-specific one. Elsewhere: meeting the general Swiss foreign-qualification subject/grade template.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Personal statements/essays -- not a standard requirement anywhere in the general Swiss route reviewed, including at St. Gallen, where the video interview (oral, not written) is the closest analogue and is again a general-HSG mechanism, not Economics/Business-specific.
countries.never_infer: Never present St. Gallen's foreign-quota selection procedure as an Economics/Business-specific admissions mechanism -- it is confirmed to apply identically to Law and International Affairs at the same institution, gated by nationality/certificate origin, not field. Never assume this mechanism generalizes to Business/Economics at Zurich, Lausanne, or Geneva -- no equivalent was found there, and St. Gallen's distinctiveness is a fact about that one institution's legal foreign-quota status, not about the Economics/Business field in Switzerland generally.

countries.scope: per-Autonomous-University -- Business runs through each AU's own general holistic mechanism, not the dedicated ranking-position gate confirmed for Medicine/Dentistry/Law
countries.description: This sharply contrasts with this package's own Medicine finding for Singapore (structurally different, via a ranking-position gate plus a mandatory standardized-test layer for Medicine/Dentistry/Law specifically). Business is not named among NUS's ranking-position-gated programmes (Medicine, Dentistry, Law, Architecture, Industrial Design, Landscape Architecture, Nursing) -- NUS's BBA instead runs through the same general holistic mechanism confirmed for most NUS programmes: up to four listed achievements/co-curricular activities plus character-limited short-response questions, with 'Aptitude-Based Admission' language reserved for exceptional candidates but explicitly subsumed into standard review for every applicant per NUS's own current page (the historical ~15% figure is superseded context, not current policy, as the existing Singapore country doc already establishes). SMU -- itself an almost entirely business/management-focused Autonomous University, structurally comparable to how St. Gallen relates to Switzerland -- runs its OWN general admissions mechanism (a 1,000-word essay, CCA record, test scores, and a shortlisted small-group interview assessing listening/reasoning rather than 'correct' answers) for essentially all of its applicants, since SMU has few programmes outside business/management/economics/law/computing/social science -- this is SMU's general institutional model, not a Business-specific overlay layered on top of something lighter. Neither NUS Business nor SMU was found to add a mechanism BEYOND what general admission at that AU already provides, unlike Medicine/Dentistry/Law's confirmed additional ranking-gate-plus-test layer.
countries.eligibility_determinants: At NUS: the general NUS holistic-review inputs (grades/qualification, achievements list, short-response questions) -- the same as most non-restricted NUS programmes, without the ranking-position gate Medicine/Dentistry/Law carry. At SMU: the general SMU inputs (essay, CCA record, test scores where the qualification requires them, interview performance for shortlisted candidates) -- SMU's standard admissions package for nearly any programme, business included by default.
countries.strengthens_application: At NUS: a strong, specific achievements list and short-response answers, exactly as for most non-restricted NUS programmes. At SMU: a clear, well-reasoned essay and strong group-interview performance (demonstrated listening and reasoning, not rehearsed 'correct' answers, per SMU's own stated interview philosophy).
countries.largely_irrelevant: At NUS Business specifically: the additional standardized-test layer (UCAT/SAT+AP) and ranking-position rule confirmed for Medicine/Dentistry/Law do not apply -- treating NUS Business as carrying the same added-mechanism weight as NUS Medicine would overstate its selectivity mechanism, even though its admission may still be highly competitive in outcome.
countries.never_infer: Never assume NUS Business shares Medicine/Dentistry/Law's confirmed ranking-position gate or mandatory standardized-test layer -- it does not; Business runs through NUS's general holistic mechanism instead. Never treat SMU's essay-and-interview-heavy process as a Business-specific overlay -- it is SMU's general institutional admissions model, applying to nearly every SMU programme by default, precisely because SMU is itself almost entirely a business/management-focused AU, the same 'field-dominant institution' pattern confirmed for St. Gallen in Switzerland. NTU's Business school (Nanyang Business School) was not independently researched to the same depth as NUS/SMU this pass and should not be assumed to follow either pattern without separate confirmation.

countries.scope: non-JUPAS pathway (the only pathway open to internationally-educated applicants, per RULE-ADMISSIONS-013) -- Business runs through the general non-JUPAS evaluation, not the mandatory-interview mechanism confirmed for Medicine
countries.description: As for every internationally-educated applicant in this package's Hong Kong research, JUPAS is categorically closed, so a Turkish or other foreign-qualification Business applicant sits in the non-JUPAS pathway by definition. Within non-JUPAS, HKU Business School was not found to carry a MANDATORY interview the way HKU Medicine's Multiple Mini Interview format is -- HKU Business's own materials confirm an interview is optional and arranged only for shortlisted applicants (individual Skype/Zoom format), a meaningfully lighter mechanism than Medicine's compulsory MMI. A personal statement is confirmed as an important input to HKU Business's admission decision (consistent with the general non-JUPAS pattern of personal statements appearing at the university/programme level), and references are also confirmed as one of the sources of information HKU Business draws on -- notable because recommendations are largely absent elsewhere in Hong Kong's system, making HKU Business one of the few confirmed exceptions in this package. None of this amounts to a dedicated NEW mechanism beyond the general non-JUPAS evaluation toolkit (transcript review, personal statement, optional interview, references) already available to any non-JUPAS programme -- a sharp contrast to Medicine's confirmed mandatory-interview-plus-explicit-ceiling finding for the same country.
countries.eligibility_determinants: Academic records (both internal and public examination results), predicted grades, personal statement, and references, evaluated against HKU's own published minimum for the qualification type -- the general non-JUPAS evidence package, with no confirmed Business-specific addition beyond what any non-JUPAS applicant already submits.
countries.strengthens_application: A strong personal statement and, where shortlisted, strong interview performance -- the interview itself is discretionary rather than a universal gate, so its absence for a given applicant is not itself a negative signal.
countries.largely_irrelevant: A mandatory interview -- unlike HKU Medicine, HKU Business's interview is optional and shortlist-only, so treating it as a universal requirement would overstate the mechanism.
countries.never_infer: Never assume HKU Business carries Medicine's mandatory MMI-format interview or explicit place-ceiling framing -- its interview is optional and shortlisted-only. Never assume references are absent from Hong Kong Business admission by analogy to the general Hong Kong finding that recommendations are largely absent -- HKU Business is a confirmed, named exception. HKUST's and CUHK's Business Schools were not independently researched to the same depth as HKU this pass and should not be assumed to follow the identical optional-interview pattern without separate confirmation.

cross_cutting_patterns: Where Economics/Business is structurally different, the difference is almost always PRESTIGE-TIER STRATIFICATION -- a separate, harder-to-reach elite inner track layered on top of an otherwise open or moderately competitive field -- rather than the capacity-constrained professional-licensure logic that drives nearly all of Medicine's structural differences in this package (government-funded training-place ceilings, mandatory clinical-aptitude tests). France's prepa-ECG/ECT-to-BCE/Ecricome-concours pathway runs alongside an open Licence Economie-Gestion in the same country; several elite US universities gate a named business school while most US universities treat Business as an ordinary major; the UK's TMUA/TARA cluster applies at a handful of quantitatively-elite departments while most UK Economics programmes require no test; the Netherlands numerus-fixus-caps the English track of a programme while the Dutch track of the identical programme stays open. This is a genuinely different SHAPE of structural difference from Medicine's, worth encoding separately: a field can be 'structurally different' in a country without that meaning the whole field is gated -- it can mean only its elite inner track is.

The identical named programme, at the identical university, teaching identical content, can be open-admission in one instruction-language track and numerus-fixus-capped in the other -- confirmed at UvA's Economics and Business Economics Bachelor's (Dutch track: no selection procedure; English track: numerus fixus at 850 places with a mandatory selection test). This is a different axis from RULE-ADMISSIONS-002 (university/programme overriding a national baseline), since there is no override across institutions or programmes here -- it is the same institution and the same programme, split purely by language track. It is also sharper than this package's existing Italy-Medicine instruction-language finding (both Italian tracks there were still restricted, just via different mechanisms): here one track is genuinely open and the other genuinely capped, for identical content. Never assume a Dutch programme's numerus-fixus status is uniform across its own language tracks without checking each one.

A field-dominant institution (one that is itself almost entirely focused on the program family in question -- St. Gallen for Economics/Business/Law in Switzerland, SMU for business/management/law/computing in Singapore) makes 'is this mechanism field-specific?' a genuinely harder question to answer than at a comprehensive university, because the institution's GENERAL admissions mechanism and the FIELD's mechanism collapse into what looks like the same thing from the applicant's point of view. The correct test, confirmed twice independently this pass, is whether the SAME mechanism applies to that institution's OTHER fields too (HSG's foreign-quota procedure applies identically to its Law and International Affairs students; SMU's essay-and-interview process applies to essentially all SMU applicants) -- if so, it is a general-institution fact wearing a field's clothing, not a field-specific mechanism, however strongly it correlates with that field in practice.

Canada's leading Commerce/Business programmes (Queen's Smith, Rotman Commerce, UBC Sauder, Schulich BBA) converge independently on the same distinct EVIDENCE-COLLECTION mechanism: a mandatory, timed, rubric-scored written-plus-video supplementary application assessing durable traits (initiative, resilience, problem-solving, teamwork, reflection) demonstrated in real time, rather than a retrospective activities-list review (the US Common App / NUS structured-achievements-list model). This sharpens RULE-ADMISSIONS-008 (extracurricular importance varies within Canada by institution) into a more specific claim: where Canadian Business programmes do weight non-academic evidence heavily, several of the most prominent ones use a genuinely different EVIDENCE TYPE from the activities-list model seen elsewhere in this package, not just a different WEIGHT on the same evidence type. Confirmed common among 4 of 5 leading English-Canadian Commerce programmes checked this pass (all but McGill Desautels, where no equivalent was found) -- common enough that a counselor should expect it by default at a top Canadian Commerce programme, not treat it as a single-school idiosyncrasy.
unresolved_questions: United States: whether Indiana Kelley's fall-2026 holistic-direct-admission process and Michigan Ross's fall-2025 First-Year-Admitting-Unit status remain in effect, and in the same form, in later cycles was not and cannot yet be confirmed -- both are recent, actively-changing policies (each explicitly dated to a specific recent cycle in this pass's own sources) rather than long-settled mechanisms, and should be reconfirmed each admissions cycle before being relied on.

Canada: whether McGill's Desautels BCom genuinely lacks an equivalent supplementary/video-application requirement, or simply was not surfaced by the searches run this pass, was not conclusively resolved -- treated as a real gap, not a confirmed absence, and should be checked directly against McGill's own admissions office before being used as a contrast point in counseling.

Netherlands: the numerus-fixus-vs-open status of Economics/Business Bachelor's programmes at other Dutch universities beyond Erasmus, Tilburg, and UvA (e.g., Groningen, Utrecht, Radboud, Maastricht, VU Amsterdam) was not independently checked this pass -- the three confirmed cases establish that capped Economics/Business programmes are common in the Netherlands, not that every Dutch university's programme is capped.

Switzerland: whether the University of Zurich's, HEC Lausanne's, or HEC Geneve's Business/Economics faculties carry any dedicated selectivity element (a local capacity cap, an entrance exam) beyond the general Swiss threshold-based Matura-equivalence model was checked only via general search, not each institution's own primary admissions pages -- read as likely-absent, not confirmed-absent.

France: whether Sciences Po's economics/social-science-adjacent programmes, or an individual Grande Ecole's own separate post-bac 'Bachelor' admissions track (bypassing the CPGE/concours route entirely, a pattern several French business schools are known to run alongside their concours-fed Programme Grande Ecole), carry materially different requirements from the BCE/Ecricome pathway documented here was not checked this pass -- a real, named gap rather than an oversight, since the task's specific lead concerned only the CPGE/concours dual-pathway question.

Singapore: NTU's Nanyang Business School was not independently researched to the same depth as NUS Business or SMU this pass -- its specific mechanism (whether it resembles NUS's ranking-gate-free general holistic model, SMU's essay-and-interview-heavy general model, or something else) is a genuine gap, consistent with the same NTU-specific gap already flagged in this package's existing Singapore country doc and Medicine research.

Hong Kong: HKUST's and CUHK's Business Schools' specific non-JUPAS mechanisms (whether they mirror HKU Business's optional-interview model) were not independently confirmed this pass -- only HKU was researched to sufficient depth.

Turkey: precise current-cycle (2026) taban puani/success-rank figures for METU's and Bilkent's Iktisat/Isletme programmes specifically were not pinned down with exact numbers this pass, though the underlying structural finding (EA score type, identical national mechanism, no special test) is confirmed via the existing country doc's own primary sourcing plus this pass's Bogazici figures.

Ireland, Australia, New Zealand: the 'no dedicated Business-specific mechanism' finding for these three countries rests primarily on Business/Commerce not being named among each country's own already-researched restricted-programme list, rather than on a fresh, independent Business-specific search this pass -- read as inherited confidence from the existing country docs, not independently re-verified to the same depth as the France/US/UK/Netherlands/Canada/Switzerland/Singapore/Hong Kong/Turkey leads this pass specifically targeted.
